subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: If a tangent to the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b) meets its major axis and minor axis at M and N respectively, then prove that a²/(CM)² + b²/(CN)² = 1, where C is the centre of the ellipse.

mark_split.label: Write the tangent at the parametric point
Find the intercepts M and N
Express cos θ and sin θ in CM, CN

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.64 — SAQ chapter 8 Ellipse, answer 75. NOT on an SSP page. Printed appearances: AP 18 · TS 18. Book p.64 prints three empty tick boxes but no numeric mark tags, so the 1+1+1+1 split here is OURS, following the four natural stages of the proof. The book itself draws a small figure beside this answer — an ellipse with axes X, Y, centre C, tangent point P, and the intercepts M (on the major axis) and N (on the minor axis) — so this card reproduces that figure, per the rule that a figure is authored where the book draws one. Ellipse is an SAQ-ONLY unit on the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.5). No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE BLM on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 are the orchestrator's back-test stand-in).

insider_note: M and N are the tangent's own x- and y-intercepts, found by the ordinary intercept method (set y = 0 for M, set x = 0 for N) — no separate formula for M and N needs to be memorised.

steps.label: Write the tangent at the parametric point
steps.margin_note: First mark. Every point on the ellipse can be written as P(θ) = (a cos θ, b sin θ).
steps.memory_tip: Start any 'tangent meets the axes' proof from the parametric point P(θ).
lines: Parametric point on the ellipse: P(θ) = (a cos θ, b sin θ)
Equation of the tangent at P(θ): (x cos θ)/a + (y sin θ)/b = 1
steps.why: Writing the tangent line in intercept form x/p + y/q = 1 makes its x- and y-intercepts p and q directly readable, which is exactly what M and N are.
common_mistakes: Writing the parametric point with sin and cos swapped.
Not rearranging the tangent into intercept form before trying to read off M and N.

steps.label: Find the intercepts M and N
steps.margin_note: Second mark. M is the tangent's x-intercept (on the major axis), N is its y-intercept (on the minor axis).
steps.memory_tip: In intercept form x/p + y/q = 1, p is the x-intercept and q is the y-intercept — read them off directly.
lines: The tangent meets the major axis (X-axis) at M and the minor axis (Y-axis) at N
⇒ X-intercept = CM = a/cos θ  and  Y-intercept = CN = b/sin θ
steps.why: Since C is the origin (the centre of the ellipse), the distances CM and CN are exactly the x- and y-intercepts of the tangent line found in step 1.
common_mistakes: Swapping which intercept is CM and which is CN.
Forgetting that CM and CN are being measured from the centre C, not from the point P(θ).

steps.label: Express cos θ and sin θ in CM, CN
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Invert the two relations from step 2 to isolate cos θ and sin θ.
steps.memory_tip: Once CM = a/cos θ is known, cos θ = a/CM follows by simply inverting.
lines: From CM = a/cos θ and CN = b/sin θ:
cos θ = a/CM  and  sin θ = b/CN
steps.why: Isolating cos θ and sin θ in terms of the two measurable lengths CM and CN sets up the identity cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 as the final step.
common_mistakes: Inverting only one of the two relations and leaving the other as CM = a/cos θ.
Mixing up a with CM or b with CN when inverting.

steps.label: Apply the identity and conclude
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 turns directly into the required identity.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever cos θ and sin θ are both isolated, squaring and adding using cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 finishes the proof.
steps.why: Substituting cos θ = a/CM and sin θ = b/CN into cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 gives exactly the identity that was to be proved.
common_mistakes: Squaring a/CM incorrectly, e.g. writing a/CM² instead of a²/(CM)².
Stopping one line early, at cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, without substituting back in terms of CM and CN.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: No marks — the question does not ask for a diagram. The book draws this figure alongside its own answer.
steps.memory_tip: M sits on the major axis, N sits on the minor axis — the tangent line joins them, touching the ellipse at P.
steps.why: The picture shows the tangent at P crossing the major axis at M and the minor axis at N, with C at the centre — the same layout the book itself draws beside this proof.
common_mistakes: Drawing M on the minor axis and N on the major axis, the reverse of the question's naming.
Drawing the tangent passing through the centre C, which a tangent line never does.
